messages.subject: Spatial density queries
messages.body_plain:
Dear team,

I was hoping to clarify a few elements of my understanding with you, specifically regarding covariates - I have read a lot but I think have just confused myself now. I am estimating leopard density in commercial farmland and I would like to also look at what environmental/anthropological factors might impact their spatial density/distribution.

Reading the various guide PDFs and other papers, I understand I can add trap specific environmental covariates to the trap file and model their influence on g0, and hence their potential influence on overall density. My understanding is that this just provides me with how that covariate influences detectability at each site and adjusts density estimates accordingly? Whereas for modelling influence of covariates on spatial density more widely across the survey area I would need to add the covariates to my mask rather than trap file? In order to add them to the mask and model influence on spatial density however, I need to have data on the covariates for all of the survey area - is that correct? For example, I know about whether lethal control is used or not on all the properties I had cameras on, but not necessarily all those in between/surrounding the immediate camera survey site, so would I be right in saying that my models would not run successfully/be useful if I tried to use this as a covariate in my mask to assess spatial density? But would still be able to look at overall density influence of this covariate by including it in the trap file? Whereas something like NDVI vegetation data across my whole survey area, including buffer, would be able to be used in a mask?

Slightly separate to this, I saw in someone's code recently (subset below) two options of models, measuring influence of covariates on g0 and on density:
### g0
# null
mLeopardg01 <- secr.fit(cptr_hst, model=g0~1, mask=mask5, detectfn=2, CL=TRUE)
# is magnitude of detection a learned response
mLeopardg02 <- secr.fit(cptr_hst, model=g0~b, mask=mask5, detectfn=2, CL=TRUE)
# is magnitude of detection affected by lethal control
mLeopardg03 <- secr.fit(cptr_hst, model=g0~Control, mask=mask5, detectfn=2, CL=TRUE)

### D
# null
mLeopardD1 <- secr.fit(cptr_hst, model=list(D~1, g0~session), mask=mask5, detectfn=2, CL=TRUE)
# is density affected by lethal control
mLeopardD2 <- secr.fit(cptr_hst, model=list(D~Control, g0~session), mask=mask5, detectfn=2, CL=TRUE)

I understood density as being derived and so I was a bit confused by this particular bit of code. If I only have one session, my understanding is that the '###D' objects would firstly not run with the current code, because g0~session would not be applicable, so if I then set g0~1 all my models would come out the same in this case as it is not impacted by anything because g0 won't differ if there is only one session, whereas if you were doing a multi-session survey you might want to explore this?

Many thanks in advance,
Jamie

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jamie,

Your understanding looks mostly correct to me.

> My understanding is that this just provides me with how that covariate influences detectability at each site and adjusts density estimates accordingly?

Yes to the first part. I wouldn't think of it as adjusting density estimates. Estimates of D will differ with and without the detection covariate but you're not modelling the relationship between density and the detection covariate in any biologically meaningful way. A covariate might have a strong effect on density (say animals are more likely to be at higher elevations) but no effect on detectability (an animal at a distance d from a high-elevation trap is as likely to be seen as an animal at the same distance d from a low-elevation trap). In that case you wouldn't say you've accounted for elevation effects on density by including it as a detection covariate.

> Whereas for modelling influence of covariates on spatial density more widely across the survey area I would need to add the covariates to my mask rather than trap file? In order to add them to the mask and model influence on spatial density however, I need to have data on the covariates for all of the survey area - is that correct?

Yes and yes. You can impute missing values if there are only a few, but you need values across the mask.

> would I be right in saying that my models would not run successfully/be useful if I tried to use this as a covariate in my mask to assess spatial density?

Yes (they would not).

> But would still be able to look at overall density influence of this covariate by including it in the trap file?

No, for the reasons given above.

> I understood density as being derived and so I was a bit confused by this particular bit of code.

You're right, if CL = TRUE then density is not modelled, covariates on D are presumably ignored, and the two models should give the same output. "session" is only applicable to multi-session models. With one session g0 ~ session is conceptually the same as g0 ~ 1. I say conceptually because secr will give an error because session is a factor variable with only one level.

Cheers,
Ian

messages.subject: Region.N seems highly dependent on mask spacing
messages.subject_clean: Region.N seems highly dependent on mask spacing
messages.body_plain:
Hello! I'm interested in using my model results to predict to a slightly larger area (despite all the caveats). Ultimately the goal is to use RSF-type covariates in the mask to better inform the predicted estimates for areas not sampled, but that will come later.

I've noticed that the region.N command gives very different results if the mask has different spacing, even if the boundaries and total area of the masks are the same. For example, I used the example code provided for the secr.fit() function to generate a detection history. I then fit a mask to the trap locations and fit a simple model. I created 3 additional masks that encompass a slightly larger area. One of those 3 has the same spacing. The other two have coarser and finer spacing, respectively.  If I run region.N() on the larger mask with the same spacing as the original mask, the results are as expected (density * area). However, I get very unexpected results for the other two masks, even though the mask summary indicates nearly exact total areas.

The obvious answer is to make sure the spacings are always the same, but it would be nice to be able to use different spacings for a variety of reasons. Any thoughts? Other than simply not doing this? Thanks!

set.seed(99801)
detectors <- make.grid (nx = 6, ny = 8, detector = "multi")
detections <- sim.capthist (detectors, popn = list(D = 10,
             buffer = 100), detectpar = list(g0 = 0.2, sigma = 25))
mask <- make.mask(traps = traps(detections), type = "trapbuffer", buffer = 150, spacing = 1 )
mask2 <- make.mask(traps = traps(detections), type = "trapbuffer", buffer = 250, spacing = 1 )
mask3 <- make.mask(traps = traps(detections), type = "trapbuffer", buffer = 250, spacing = 5 )
mask4 <- make.mask(traps = traps(detections), type = "trapbuffer", buffer = 250, spacing = 0.5 )

summary(mask) # 15.67 ha
summary(mask2) # 33.03 ha
summary(mask3) # 33.05 ha
summary(mask4) # 33.04 ha

secr0 <- secr.fit (detections, mask = mask)
secr0 # D = 13.88

region.N(secr0, region = mask) # E(N) = 217 (as expected)
region.N(secr0, region = mask2) # E(N) = 458 (as expected)
region.N(secr0, region = mask3) # E(N) = 18
region.N(secr0, region = mask4) # E(N) = 1834

messages.subject_clean: Region.N seems highly dependent on mask spacing
messages.body_plain:
You have found a simple bug in that corner of region.N. The code used the cell size of the original mask rather than cell size of the region mask. I have fixed this in the version on GitHub, and in principle you can install from there, but it may be simpler to wait a few days for it to find its way onto CRAN.

Now I get -

R.N 217.5217    29.89550 168.4534 287.0892 51

> region.N(secr0, region = mask2) # E(N) = 458 (as expected)

    estimate SE.estimate      lcl      ucl  n
E.N 458.6269    70.28544 340.2261 618.2319 51
R.N 458.6270    66.94338 347.0749 612.2085 51

> region.N(secr0, region = mask3) # E(N) = 18

    estimate SE.estimate      lcl      ucl  n
E.N 458.8157    70.31437 340.3662 618.4864 51
R.N 458.8158    66.97235 347.2149 612.4630 51

> region.N(secr0, region = mask4) # E(N) = 1834

    estimate SE.estimate      lcl      ucl  n
E.N 458.6269    70.28544 340.2261 618.2319 51
R.N 458.6270    66.94338 347.0749 612.2085 51

Thanks for reporting this.
Murray

Thanks a lot for confirming and clarifying Ian.

So just finally, on that first point.

> My understanding is that this just provides me with how that covariate influences detectability at each site and adjusts density estimates accordingly?
Yes to the first part. I wouldn't think of it as adjusting density estimates. Estimates of D will differ with and without the detection covariate but you're not modelling the relationship between density and the detection covariate in any biologically meaningful way. A covariate might have a strong effect on density (say animals are more likely to be at higher elevations) but no effect on detectability (an animal at a distance d from a high-elevation trap is as likely to be seen as an animal at the same distance d from a low-elevation trap). In that case you wouldn't say you've accounted for elevation effects on density by including it as a detection covariate.

As I understand it, if my model that includes a covariate for 'use of lethal control' estimates density at 2.21 and my null model 2.5 for example, the conclusion is that, given what we know about lethal control in the area, 2.21 is a more likely density estimate.

Is that the right idea?

Thanks
Jamie

messages.body_plain:
Hi Joe
I don't have an answer, I'm afraid. I assume this is a spatial model and has taken forever? Someone should research strategies for large datasets. I have some myself that are too long to be practical in one sweep, hence the (unproven) function moving.fit(). No doubt a Bayesian approach would work, partly because it is less fussy about finding a unique solution. With that in mind, it seems reasonable to accept an almost-maximized ML result. Murray
